listeningParts.title: Booking a farm-stay holiday
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a farm that offers holiday accommodation.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Hello, Brookfield Farm, Sarah speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh hi, I saw your website and I'm interested in booking a farm holiday for my family. Could you tell me a bit about what you offer?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Of course. We've got three holiday cottages on the farm. Two of them sleep four people, and the larger one, which is called the Old Barn, sleeps six.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: There are five of us, me, my husband and three children, so I guess we'd need the Old Barn.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Yes, that would be best. It has three bedrooms, two bathrooms and a big kitchen. All our cottages are self-catering, but we do sell eggs, milk and vegetables from the farm shop, and there's a village shop about two miles away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Sounds lovely. What sort of farm is it?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Mainly dairy. We milk about a hundred and twenty cows. We also keep a small flock of sheep, some pigs and chickens, and the children usually love the goats.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Can the kids help with the animals?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: They can. Every morning at eight we have what we call the farm walk. Guests can come with me to collect the eggs and feed the calves and the goats. It lasts about an hour. It's included in the price, but children have to be accompanied by an adult.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Can they watch the cows being milked?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a viewing gallery above the milking parlour. Milking happens twice a day, at half past five in the morning and four in the afternoon. Most families prefer the afternoon one, for obvious reasons.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I can imagine. Now, we were thinking about the first week of August. Is the Old Barn available?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Let me look. I'm afraid the first week of August is booked. But it's free the following week, from Saturday the ninth to Saturday the sixteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That should be okay. What's the price for that week?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: In August, the Old Barn is nine hundred and seventy-five pounds for the week. That includes bed linen, towels, heating and electricity.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's within our budget. Is there anything extra to pay for?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Only if you bring a dog, which is fifteen pounds for the week. And we can provide a cot or a high chair if you have a baby, at no extra charge.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No dog and no baby, thankfully. What else is there to do in the area?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Lots. The coast is about twenty minutes' drive. There's a lovely sandy beach at Westbay. And if you like walking, there's a footpath that goes right through the farm along the river to the castle. Cycling is popular too. We have bikes guests can borrow, though we don't have any child seats.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My youngest is nine, so she can ride her own bike. Do we need a car while we're there?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: It helps, because buses are only every two hours. But if you come by train, I can collect you from the station at Millbridge. There's a charge of ten pounds each way for that.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll probably drive, but that's useful to know. How do I book?

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: You can book online, or I can take your details now. We ask for a deposit of twenty-five per cent when you book, and the rest four weeks before you arrive. If you cancel more than eight weeks before, you get the deposit back.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Let's do it now. My name's Karen Whitlock, W-H-I-T-L-O-C-K.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Lovely, Karen. And how did you hear about us?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: A friend of mine stayed with you last year. She said it was the best holiday her kids had ever had.

dialogue.speaker: Owner
dialogue.text: Oh, that's nice to hear. Let me take your card details for the deposit.

listeningParts.title: Opening day at the city farm
listeningParts.contextDescription: The manager of a community city farm speaks to visitors at an open day.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Riverside City Farm's annual open day. I'm Grace Hollis, the farm manager. Thanks for joining us, especially those of you who came despite the rain. I'll tell you a little about the farm and the programme for today, and then you're free to explore.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The farm was started thirty years ago by a group of local residents who wanted to turn an abandoned railway yard into something useful for the community. In the early days, it was run entirely by volunteers. Today we have eight paid staff, but volunteers are still at the heart of everything we do. Last year, over two hundred people gave their time, from schoolchildren to retired engineers.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Our main purpose is education. Many children growing up in the city have never seen a cow or a pig up close, and some don't really know where their food comes from. So every week during term time, we welcome school groups, and our education centre runs sessions on everything from bread-making to bees. We also offer apprenticeships for young people who want a career in agriculture or animal care. Three of last year's apprentices have now got full-time jobs on commercial farms.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We're particularly proud of our rare breeds. Many traditional breeds of farm animals have almost disappeared because modern farms prefer breeds that grow faster or produce more milk. But these older breeds often have valuable qualities: they may be hardier, more resistant to disease, or better suited to grazing poor land. We keep several, including Tamworth pigs and Bagot goats, and we work with a national charity to help keep these breeds going.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, a quick guide to today's activities. The sheep-shearing demonstration takes place in the main barn at eleven o'clock. Please don't be alarmed; it doesn't hurt the sheep at all, and in fact they're much more comfortable without their heavy winter coats.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: At twelve, there's a talk on composting in the vegetable garden by our head gardener, Tom. Everything we grow here is fertilised with compost made from animal manure and garden waste. Tom will explain how you can make your own at home, even if you only have a small balcony.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Children's activities are in the education centre all day. There's pond-dipping, where children can look for insects and small creatures in our pond, and egg-decorating, which is always popular. Please note that the pony rides, which were advertised on our leaflet, have had to be cancelled, because the field is too wet after this week's rain. We're very sorry about that.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: For older children and adults, there's also a guided tour of the farm every hour, starting at the main gate. Our volunteers will explain how we care for the animals and how the farm is run. The tours are free, but numbers are limited to fifteen people, so please collect a ticket from the information tent first.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Food is available at the café, which uses vegetables from our garden and eggs from our own hens. All profits go towards running the farm. There's also a plant sale outside the café, where you can buy seedlings that our volunteers have grown.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Finally, a few requests. Please wash your hands after touching any animals. There are sinks by every animal pen. Don't feed the animals anything you've brought with you, as some ordinary foods can make them quite ill; you can buy bags of suitable animal feed from the shop. And dogs, I'm afraid, must stay outside the farm gates, because they can frighten the animals.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Oh, and if you've enjoyed your visit, we'd love you to think about volunteering. There's a stand by the entrance where you can find out more. Thank you, and enjoy the day.

listeningParts.title: A project on cattle and methane
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two agriculture students, Nadia and Ben, talk to their tutor about a research project on reducing methane from cattle.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Nadia, Ben, you've chosen methane emissions from cattle for your project. Tell me why.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: Well, I grew up on a dairy farm, so I'm interested in anything that affects farmers. And we kept reading that cattle are a major source of greenhouse gases. We wanted to understand how much of that is true, and what farmers can actually do about it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: And it's a topic that combines biology and economics, which suits both of us. Nadia's done more animal science, and I've done more on farm business.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. So what have you found out so far?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: The basic science first. Cattle produce methane in the rumen, the first part of their stomach, where microbes break down grass and other plant material. Most people think the methane comes out the back end, but in fact about ninety per cent is breathed out or belched.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. And what approaches are there to reducing it?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: We've grouped them into three. First, feed additives. There's a lot of research on a type of red seaweed which can cut methane dramatically in trials. The problem is that it's difficult to grow in large quantities, and it isn't clear yet whether the effect lasts over months. There's also a synthetic additive that has been approved in some countries, and it seems to give a reduction of about a third.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the second group?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Breeding. Some animals naturally produce less methane than others, and that seems to be partly inherited. So in theory, farmers could select bulls whose daughters produce less. The advantage is that the change is permanent and cumulative. The disadvantage is that it's slow; it would take many generations to make a big difference.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: And the third is improving efficiency in general. If cows are healthier and produce more milk each, you need fewer cows to produce the same amount of milk, so total emissions fall even if each cow produces the same amount of methane.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point. Which approach do you think is most promising?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: Honestly, I think efficiency is the most realistic in the short term, because farmers already have reasons to do it. It saves them money.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: I'm more interested in the additives. If the cost comes down, they could be added to feed on almost any farm without changing anything else.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Have you thought about how the different approaches might be combined?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: Not yet, but that's a good idea. A farmer could improve efficiency now, use additives when they become cheaper, and choose low-methane bulls at the same time. The effects might add up.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Though we'd need to check whether anyone has actually measured the combined effect. It might not simply add up.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: It sounds like you'll have plenty to discuss. Now, for the primary research part, what were you planning?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: We wanted to interview farmers. My family know a lot of farmers locally, so getting people to talk to us shouldn't be difficult.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's useful, but be careful. If all your interviewees are friends of your family, they may not be typical. Try to include a range: different sizes of farm, organic and conventional, perhaps some beef as well as dairy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We could also send a short online questionnaire through the farmers' union. That would reach more people.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good idea. The interviews will give you depth, and the questionnaire will give you numbers. What would you ask?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: Mainly whether they'd be willing to use additives, and what would stop them. My guess is cost.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Perhaps. But don't assume. Ask an open question first, before you suggest any answers. Farmers may surprise you; some may be more worried about whether the milk will taste different, or about what supermarkets will say.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: That's a good point. We'll pilot the questions with two farmers first and see what comes up.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. Send me your interview questions by Friday and we'll go through them.

listeningParts.title: The domestication of animals
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an archaeology and animal science course.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In today's lecture, I want to look at one of the most important developments in human history: the domestication of animals. Almost all the meat, milk, wool and leather people use today comes from a handful of species that were domesticated thousands of years ago. So, I'll consider when and where this happened, how it may have happened, and why so few species were ever domesticated.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's begin with the dog, which was the first animal to be domesticated, long before any farm animal. Dogs descend from a population of wolves, and genetic evidence suggests that domestication began at least fifteen thousand years ago, possibly much earlier, when humans were still hunters and gatherers. One popular theory is that some wolves began following human groups to feed on leftovers, and that the less fearful animals gradually became tamer over many generations. In other words, the wolves may have domesticated themselves to some extent.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The main farm animals came later, after the beginning of agriculture. Sheep and goats were domesticated around eleven thousand years ago in the region known as the Fertile Crescent, which stretches from what is now Iraq through Syria to Turkey. Cattle followed soon after, from a large wild animal called the aurochs, which was much bigger and more aggressive than modern cattle. The aurochs survived in the forests of Europe until 1627, when the last known animal died in Poland. Pigs were domesticated separately in at least two regions: the Middle East and China.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: How do we know all this? Traditionally, archaeologists relied on bones found at ancient settlements. Domestic animals tend to be smaller than their wild ancestors, so a reduction in the size of bones over time is one sign of domestication. Another clue is age. When people hunt wild animals, they kill animals of all ages, but herders tend to slaughter mainly young males and keep females for breeding. So if most of the bones at a site come from young males, it suggests the animals were being managed. More recently, analysis of ancient DNA has transformed the field, allowing researchers to trace the movement of domestic animals as farming spread.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So why were so few species domesticated? Of the roughly one hundred and fifty large plant-eating mammals in the world, only fourteen were domesticated before the twentieth century. The geographer Jared Diamond argued that a species needs several characteristics to be a good candidate. It must be able to live on food that humans can easily provide, such as grass. It must grow quickly and breed easily in captivity; animals like elephants take too long to reach adulthood. It must not be too aggressive or too nervous; zebras, for example, are notoriously bad-tempered and difficult to handle, and gazelles tend to panic in enclosures and injure themselves. And finally, it helps if the animal lives naturally in herds with a clear social hierarchy, because then humans can take the place of the leader.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Domestication changed the animals in many ways. Over centuries of selective breeding, farmers chose animals with desirable traits, so that modern sheep produce far more wool than wild sheep, and modern dairy cows produce many times as much milk as their ancestors. Interestingly, domestic animals of very different species share certain features, such as floppy ears, patches of white in their coat, and smaller brains relative to body size. Scientists call this the domestication syndrome, and one theory is that selecting animals for tameness accidentally affected other traits at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Domestication changed humans too. Living close to animals exposed people to new diseases, many of which, such as measles, probably originated in livestock. And in populations that relied heavily on dairy farming, adults gradually developed the ability to digest milk, something most mammals lose after infancy. Next week, we'll look at how modern genetics is changing livestock breeding today.

readingPassages.title: The humble potato
paragraphs: Today the potato is the world's most important food crop after rice, wheat and maize, grown in more than one hundred and fifty countries and eaten in almost every cuisine. Yet five hundred years ago it was unknown outside South America. The potato was first domesticated in the Andes mountains, around Lake Titicaca on the border of present-day Peru and Bolivia, perhaps seven or eight thousand years ago. Andean farmers developed thousands of varieties, adapted to different altitudes and soils, in a remarkable range of shapes and colours, from tiny purple tubers to long yellow ones. Many of these traditional varieties are still grown in Andean villages today, where a single farmer may cultivate dozens of types in one field, partly as a precaution against pests and bad weather.

Potatoes were well suited to the harsh conditions of the high Andes, where few other crops could grow. Andean peoples also developed an ingenious way of preserving them. Potatoes were left outside to freeze overnight in the cold mountain air and then trampled to squeeze out the water, before being dried in the sun. The result, known as chuño, could be stored for years without spoiling and provided a vital reserve of food in times of poor harvests. The Inca state, which controlled much of the Andes in the fifteenth century, kept large stores of chuño to feed its armies and workers.

Spanish invaders reached the Andes in the 1530s, and potatoes probably arrived in Europe some time in the 1570s. At first, Europeans were suspicious of the new food. The potato belongs to the same plant family as the poisonous nightshade, and its leaves and green parts are indeed toxic. Some people believed that potatoes caused disease, while others objected that they were not mentioned in the Bible. For many decades, they were grown mainly as a curiosity in botanical gardens or as food for animals and the poor. Their unfamiliar appearance did not help: unlike grain, which had been the basis of European diets for thousands of years, potatoes grew hidden underground, and some farmers were unsure how to plant or store them.

Attitudes gradually changed, partly as a result of deliberate promotion by governments. In Prussia, King Frederick the Great ordered his subjects to plant potatoes in the 1750s, recognising that they could help prevent famine. In France, the scientist Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, who had eaten potatoes as a prisoner of war, campaigned tirelessly to persuade his countrymen of their value. According to a popular story, he had a field of potatoes guarded by soldiers during the day, but left unguarded at night, so that local people would assume the crop was valuable and steal it.

By the nineteenth century, the potato had become a staple food across much of northern Europe. Its advantages were considerable. An acre of potatoes could feed far more people than an acre of wheat, and potatoes grew well in cool, wet climates and poor soils. Some historians argue that the spread of the potato was one of the main reasons for the rapid growth of Europe's population in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, which in turn provided workers for the expanding industrial cities.

However, heavy dependence on a single crop brought great risks. In Ireland, a large part of the rural population relied on potatoes for almost all of their food, and most farmers grew just one or two varieties. When a disease known as potato blight arrived in 1845, it destroyed crops across the country for several years in succession. The resulting famine killed around a million people, and a similar number emigrated, mainly to North America. The disaster was made far worse by government policies, but its scale also reflected the lack of genetic diversity in the potatoes being grown.

Today, scientists are once again looking to the Andes. The International Potato Centre in Lima, Peru, maintains a collection of more than four thousand varieties, including many wild relatives of the cultivated potato. These plants carry genes for resistance to disease, drought and extreme temperatures that may prove essential as farmers adapt to a changing climate. The lesson of the Irish famine, that diversity is a form of insurance, has never been more relevant.

readingPassages.title: Rethinking animal welfare on the farm
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, the welfare of farm animals was judged mainly by their physical health and productivity. A cow that produced plenty of milk, or a hen that laid regularly, was assumed to be well looked after. This view was challenged in 1964 by the publication of Animal Machines, a book by the British writer Ruth Harrison, which described the conditions in the new intensive farming systems that were spreading rapidly after the Second World War. Harrison's account of calves kept in narrow crates and hens confined in small cages caused widespread public concern.

In response, the British government set up a committee of experts, led by the zoologist Roger Brambell, to investigate. Its report, published in 1965, argued that animals should at least have the freedom to turn around, groom themselves, get up, lie down and stretch their limbs. These ideas were later developed into what became known as the Five Freedoms: freedom from hunger and thirst; from discomfort; from pain, injury and disease; from fear and distress; and the freedom to express normal behaviour. The Five Freedoms have since been adopted as the basis for animal welfare law and farm assurance schemes in many countries.

In recent decades, however, many animal welfare scientists have argued that the Five Freedoms do not go far enough. Their central criticism is that the framework focuses almost entirely on preventing negative experiences. An animal might be free from hunger, pain and fear, yet still live a dull and unrewarding life. Researchers such as David Mellor in New Zealand have proposed an alternative approach, the Five Domains model, which considers nutrition, environment, health and behaviour, and then asks how these affect the animal's mental state. Crucially, it encourages farmers to provide opportunities for positive experiences, such as play, exploration and comfort.

But how can we know what an animal is experiencing? Scientists have developed a number of methods. One is to measure physical indicators of stress, such as heart rate or levels of hormones in the blood. Another is to observe behaviour: animals in poor conditions often show repetitive movements with no obvious purpose, such as pacing or chewing the bars of a pen. A third approach is to offer animals choices and measure how hard they are willing to work for something. In one series of experiments, hens were required to push through increasingly heavy doors to reach different resources. They worked hard to reach a secluded nest box before laying an egg, suggesting that nesting is something they strongly need.

Positive emotions are harder to measure, but progress is being made. Calves and young pigs play more when they are healthy and comfortable, and play tends to disappear when conditions are poor, so it may serve as a useful sign of good welfare. Some researchers have also used what is called qualitative behaviour assessment, in which trained observers describe the overall body language of a group of animals using terms such as 'relaxed', 'curious' or 'agitated'. Although this may sound subjective, studies have found that different observers tend to agree closely.

Improving welfare can have practical benefits for farmers as well as animals. Stress and disease reduce growth and milk yield, and animals that are calm are easier and safer to handle. On the other hand, some higher-welfare systems require more space or labour, which raises costs, and consumers do not always choose to pay more for the resulting products. Surveys regularly find that most shoppers say they care about animal welfare, but sales of higher-welfare products remain well below what those surveys would suggest.

This gap between what people say and what they buy has led some experts to argue that welfare cannot be left to consumer choice alone. They call for clearer labelling, so that shoppers can understand the conditions in which animals were kept, and for minimum legal standards that apply to all producers. Others warn that if standards in one country rise too far above those elsewhere, production may simply move abroad, with no overall benefit for animals. What is clear is that the scientific understanding of animal minds has advanced considerably since Ruth Harrison's book, and that this understanding is changing the questions that farmers, consumers and governments must answer.

readingPassages.title: Can vertical farms feed the cities?
paragraphs: In a converted warehouse on the edge of a European city, lettuces are growing in trays stacked twelve layers high, lit by rows of pink-tinged LED lamps. There is no soil and no sunlight; the plants' roots hang in a nutrient solution that is pumped through the system and recycled, and the temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide levels are controlled by computer. Supporters of this kind of vertical farming describe it as the future of agriculture. Sceptics regard it as an expensive way of growing salad, and point to a string of companies that have failed after promising to transform the food system. The truth, I would argue, lies somewhere between these positions.

The case for vertical farming begins with land. The world's population is expected to approach ten billion by the middle of the century, and much of the land best suited to agriculture is already in use. By growing upwards rather than outwards, a vertical farm can produce many times as much food per square metre as a field. Because the environment is controlled, crops can be grown all year round, regardless of the weather, and harvests are highly predictable. Vertical farms use no pesticides, since insects and diseases can largely be kept out, and they use up to ninety-five per cent less water than conventional farms, because water is recycled rather than lost to evaporation and drainage.

Location is another advantage. Vertical farms can be built in or close to cities, where most consumers live. This reduces the distance that food must travel, and allows produce to reach shops within hours of harvest, when it is at its freshest. In places with very limited farmland or extreme climates, such as Singapore or the Gulf states, which currently import most of their fresh vegetables, local vertical farms could make food supplies more secure.

The central problem is energy. In a field, sunlight is free. In a vertical farm, every unit of light has to be supplied by electricity, and lighting typically accounts for the largest share of running costs. Although LED lamps have become far more efficient, a vertical farm still uses vastly more energy per kilogram of produce than a greenhouse, let alone a field. If that electricity comes from fossil fuels, the environmental benefits of using less land and water may be cancelled out by higher carbon emissions. The rise in energy prices in Europe after 2021 forced several high-profile vertical farming companies to close or reduce their operations, despite having attracted hundreds of millions of dollars from investors.

Energy costs also limit what can sensibly be grown. Leafy greens such as lettuce, herbs and spinach are well suited to vertical farms: they grow quickly, are mostly water, and have a high value relative to their weight. Staple crops are a different matter. A field of wheat requires enormous amounts of light energy, and one calculation suggested that producing a loaf of bread in a vertical farm would cost many times its normal price in electricity alone. For the foreseeable future, it seems very unlikely that vertical farms will grow the cereals, beans and potatoes that provide most of the world's calories.

This does not mean that the technology is unimportant. Research in vertical farms has greatly improved our understanding of how plants respond to light of different colours, and some of this knowledge is already being applied in conventional greenhouses. Vertical farms may also have a valuable role in producing young plants for transplanting into fields, which gives farmers a head start in the growing season, and in growing high-value crops such as medicinal plants, or plants for research, where precise control of growing conditions is more important than cost. And as renewable electricity becomes cheaper and more widely available, the economics of vertical farming may improve.

Perhaps the most sensible conclusion is that vertical farms should be seen as one tool among many rather than a replacement for traditional agriculture. Feeding a growing population will depend far more on reducing food waste, improving yields on existing farmland and protecting soils than on stacking lettuces in warehouses. Nevertheless, in the right places and for the right crops, vertical farming could make a modest but useful contribution to a more resilient food system.

writingTask1.title: Milk production on a dairy farm
writingTask1.instructions: The diagram below shows how milk is produced and processed, from the farm to the supermarket. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
processSteps: Cows graze on pasture or are fed silage in winter
Cows are milked twice a day by machine
Milk is cooled to 4°C in a tank on the farm
A tanker collects the milk every two days
At the dairy, milk is tested for quality
Milk is pasteurised: heated to 72°C for 15 seconds
Cream is separated to produce skimmed or semi-skimmed milk
Milk is bottled, labelled and delivered to supermarkets
